screens.title: Speculative Execution and the Limits of Dynamic Scheduling
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we will explore why modern processors make educated guesses and how those guesses can both accelerate and complicate execution. Speculative execution lets a C P U execute instructions before dependencies or branch directions are certain. When predictions are correct, work is committed quickly and throughput rises. When predictions are wrong, the processor discards speculative results and pays a recovery cost. You will learn the role of the reorder buffer in delaying commits until program order is safe, how memory disambiguation allows loads to run early, and why techniques like store set prediction can improve or harm performance depending on accuracy. We will also quantify the trade-offs: accuracy versus recovery cost versus performance gain, using an expected-gain inequality to judge profitability. Finally, you will reflect on real limits — security issues such as Spectre and Meltdown, power consumption, and diminishing returns — and how architects balance speed and safety. By the end, you should be able to reason about when speculation is a net win and when designers must pull back.

screens.title: Branch Prediction & Speculative Execution — The Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Speculative execution begins with branch prediction: the processor guesses which path a branch will take and continues fetching and executing instructions along that guessed path. Define speculative execution as executing instructions before their validity is confirmed, and branch prediction as the mechanism that makes the guesses. A concrete example: when a conditional jump depends on a register loaded from memory, early fetching of both the predicted path instructions and their operands keeps decode and execution units busy while the branch resolves. This produces performance when the predictor is correct because the pipeline avoids stalls and work is committed with little delay. A common misconception is to assume that speculative execution changes program semantics — it does not. Speculative results are kept separate from the architectural state until a commit, so incorrect speculations are discarded, and the program-level behavior remains the same. The key takeaway is that speculation increases throughput but requires mechanisms to track, validate, and discard work when predictions fail. Reflect: what kind of workload would gain most from accurate branch prediction? Branch Prediction & Speculative Execution — The Basics means speculative execution performs work based on predictions; correct predictions save cycles, incorrect ones require recovery but do not change program correctness.. In practical terms, how guessing branch outcomes keeps pipelines busy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Branch Prediction Basics
Core Concept

Branch prediction enables speculative work

Processors guess branch outcomes to fetch and execute from a predicted path, avoiding stalls when guesses are correct.

Concrete example
A conditional jump whose condition depends on a load can be guessed; subsequent instructions execute while the load completes.
Common misconception
Speculation does not change program results because commits occur only after correctness is confirmed.
Key Takeaway
Branch prediction improves throughput when accuracy is high enough that recovery cost is outweighed by saved stalls.
Visual checklist
  • Predict branch direction
  • Fetch from predicted path
  • Execute speculatively, mark results as speculative
  • Commit only after branch resolution
  • Flush on misprediction
Check your understanding
Name one workload trait that makes branch prediction especially valuable, and explain why.

screens.title: The Reorder Buffer (ROB) — Ensuring In-order Commit
screens.narratorSegment: The reorder buffer, or ROB, is the structure that lets processors execute out of order while still committing results in program order. Conceptually it is a circular buffer that holds each instruction from issue until commit. When an instruction completes out of order, its result is written into the ROB entry, not yet into the register file or memory. Only when the instruction reaches the head of the ROB and all prior instructions are committed does the processor write its result to the architectural state. This design guarantees precise exceptions: if an exception or misprediction occurs, the ROB can be flushed back to a known safe state because no speculative results have modified the visible state. A concrete example: a speculative instruction that computed a register value waits in the ROB; if the branch that enabled it mispredicts, that ROB entry is discarded and no architectural register is modified. A common misconception is that out-of-order execution commits results as they finish — it does not. The ROB is the gatekeeper. The main takeaway is that the ROB decouples execution completion from architectural commitment, enabling both performance and correctness.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Reorder Buffer (ROB)
Definition

ROB holds speculative results until commit

A circular buffer that maintains program order for commits and supports precise exception handling.

How it works
  1. Instruction issued and allocated an ROB entry.
  2. Instruction executes out of order and writes results to the ROB entry.
  3. When entry reaches head and previous commits done, result is written architecturally.
  4. On misprediction, speculative entries are flushed.
Concrete example
A speculative ALU result is stored in its ROB slot until the branch is resolved; if the branch is wrong, the slot is discarded and the register file is unchanged.
Why it matters
The ROB lets architects decouple execution ordering from visible state updates, enabling aggressive out-of-order execution while preserving correctness and precise exceptions.
Key takeaway
ROB entries are the safe ledger of speculative work — they allow rollbacks and precise program-visible behavior.

screens.title: Speculative State Lifecycle and Flush on Misprediction
screens.narratorSegment: Speculative state follows a lifecycle from fetch to commit. First, the branch predictor suggests a path and the fetch stage brings in instructions. Those instructions are allocated ROB entries and are allowed to execute out of order in reservation stations. When an instruction produces a result, it writes into its ROB slot marked speculative. The branch resolution event clears speculation bits if the path was correct; then entries become eligible to commit in program order. If the branch is wrong, all speculative ROB entries after the mispredicted branch are flushed and their work is discarded. Consider an example: a sequence of instructions after a predicted taken branch executes and populates ROB entries; branch resolves as not taken — the pipeline must discard those entries and fetch the right path, incurring refill latency. A common misconception is that flushing simply wastes a few cycles; in practice, the recovery cost includes pipeline refill, lost cache prefetch benefits, and wasted execution bandwidth. The takeaway: the lifecycle enforces correctness but determines recovery cost, so architects aim to reduce both misprediction rates and flush penalties.

keyIdea.title: Speculative lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Speculative instructions are fetched, executed, stored in the ROB, and either committed or flushed depending on branch resolution; flushes cause recovery costs beyond just cycles wasted.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Speculative Lifecycle
Process Flow

Fetch → Execute(speculative) → ROB store → Commit/Flush

1. Fetch & predict
Predict branch and fetch from predicted path.
2. Execute speculatively
Instructions execute out of order; results go to ROB entries.
3. Resolve & commit
If prediction correct, entries clear speculation and commit in order.
Concrete scenario
A misprediction causes flushing of ROB entries after the branch. The pipeline must discard speculative results and refill from the correct path, incurring cycles lost and possibly warming caches for the wrong data.
Misconception
Flushing seems cheap but includes refill and lost speculative side-effects such as prefetches, making recovery cost meaningful.
Key Takeaway
The lifecycle enforces correctness but also determines the recovery penalty on misprediction; architects design predictors and ROB behavior to minimize net loss.

screens.title: Memory Disambiguation: Techniques Compared
screens.narratorSegment: Memory disambiguation addresses the question: can a load execute before earlier stores reveal their addresses? There are three primary strategies described in the chapter. First, address-based disambiguation compares computed store addresses against load addresses as soon as they become available. If they match, the load is re-executed or forwarded with correct data. This is precise but requires waiting for store addresses or checking them later. Second, store set prediction records which stores previously caused conflicts with a given load and predicts future conflicts, enabling the load to avoid executing early when likely to alias. This can increase performance if the predictor is accurate. Third, conservative scheduling simply delays loads until all prior store addresses are known; it is safe but limits parallelism. A concrete example: a load that frequently conflicts with a recent store benefits from store set prediction; a load that rarely aliases should be allowed early execution. A common misconception is thinking a single technique suits all workloads. In practice, architects combine mechanisms: fast predictions for common cases, precise checks to recover from mispredictions, and conservative fallbacks for uncertain situations. The takeaway is that memory-disambiguation design affects both performance and complexity.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Memory Disambiguation
Comparison

Three approaches

Address-based disambiguation
Compare store and load addresses when available; re-execute or forward if they match.
Store set prediction
Predict which stores a load might conflict with using historical conflict patterns.
Conservative scheduling
Delay loads until prior store addresses are known — safe, but reduces parallelism.
Concrete example
A load that often reads the same address as a recent store benefits from store set prediction to avoid stalls. If prediction misses, the load is replayed or forwarded when the store address becomes known.
Key takeaway
Mixing a fast predictor with precise address checks gives performance while retaining correctness through replay or forwarding on conflicts.

screens.title: Memory Dependence Speculation — Why it Matters
screens.narratorSegment: Memory dependence speculation lets loads run before prior stores' addresses are known. This is powerful because many loads do not actually depend on earlier stores; running them early uncovers more instruction-level parallelism and often reduces critical-path latency. For a concrete example imagine a load whose address typically differs from recent stores; allowing it to run five cycles earlier can directly shorten execution time if the load lies on the critical path. The risk is that a misprediction requires the load and its dependent instructions to be replayed, which can be expensive. A common misconception is to assume all loads benefit equally; they do not. Only loads that are likely independent and on the critical path offer meaningful gains. The chapter emphasizes that accurate prediction and efficient forwarding or replay mechanisms are essential. The takeaway is simple: memory dependence speculation is one of the most performance-critical designs in aggressive out-of-order processors, and its profitability hinges on accurate conflict prediction and low replay cost. In practical terms, how speculative loads can change throughput and where the risk lies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Memory Dependence Speculation
Definition

Speculative loads before stores are resolved

If a load is predicted not to alias earlier stores, it runs early and may be forwarded data or replayed later if wrong.

Concrete example
A load that usually reads a distinct address executes five cycles earlier, reducing critical path latency by those cycles when correct.
Misconception
Not every load should be speculated; benefits depend on alias patterns and whether the load lies on the critical path.
Why it matters
Because memory dependence speculation often yields bigger performance wins than other speculation forms, it receives special hardware attention in high-performance processors.

screens.title: Expected Gain Inequality — Quantifying Profitability
screens.narratorSegment: We can reason about speculation profitability with a simple expected-gain inequality. The expected gain from speculation equals Accuracy multiplied by the gain when correct, and the expected cost equals the misprediction rate multiplied by the recovery cost. The inequality is Accuracy × Gain_when_correct > (1 − Accuracy) × Cost_when_wrong. A concrete calculation from the chapter: if branch prediction is 95% accurate and a misprediction costs 15 cycles, the expected cost per branch is 0.05 × 15 = 0.75 cycles. If the correct prediction avoids a 1-cycle stall, the expected gain (0.95 × 1 = 0.95 cycles) exceeds the expected cost, so speculation is profitable. A common misconception is that high accuracy alone guarantees value; you must compare expected gain to expected cost for your workload. The practical takeaway is to always compute expected gain per speculation and weigh it against pipeline refill and replay penalties. The visual code panel shows the formula and a short numeric example for clarity. content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Expected Gain
Formula
<!-- Expected gain inequality -->
Expected Gain = Accuracy × Gain_when_correct
Expected Cost = (1 - Accuracy) × Cost_when_wrong
Profit if: Accuracy × Gain_when_correct > (1 - Accuracy) × Cost_when_wrong

# numeric example:
Accuracy = 0.95
Gain_when_correct = 1  # cycle saved
Cost_when_wrong = 15   # cycles lost on mispredict
Expected Gain = 0.95 × 1 = 0.95
Expected Cost = 0.05 × 15 = 0.75
Profit = Expected Gain - Expected Cost = 0.20 cycles per branch
Concrete note
Even small positive expected gains add up across many branches. But if recovery cost or misprediction rate rises, the same calculation can flip and make speculation unprofitable.
Key takeaway
Always compute expected gain for your specific workload; accuracy alone is not sufficient to decide.

screens.title: Compute CPI and Speedup for Branch-heavy Workloads
screens.narratorSegment: Let's work through the hands-on calculation given in the chapter to make the expected-gain thinking concrete. The workload has 20% branches and the processor can execute 4 instructions per cycle. Without speculation the processor stalls on every branch for 2 cycles, so the branch-related CPI penalty per instruction stream is 0.20 × 2 = 0.4 cycles per instruction. With speculation, correct predictions avoid the 2-cycle stall but mispredictions cost 15 cycles. For a predictor with 90% accuracy: misprediction rate is 0.10, expected penalty per branch = 0.10 × 15 = 1.5 cycles; per instruction penalty = 0.20 × 1.5 = 0.30 cycles. Combine with base CPI (assuming ideal CPI = 1 / IPC = 0.25 cycles per instruction if 4 IPC), you can compute effective CPI with and without speculation and derive speedup. Repeat for 95% and 99% accuracy to see how quickly marginal returns rise. A common misconception is that higher accuracy always yields linear speedup; in reality, diminishing returns appear because the base pipeline and other bottlenecks begin to dominate. The final step is comparing effective CPI numbers to decide whether speculation yields worthwhile program-level speedup.

Module 6 › Chapter 5.7 › Hands-on CPI
Problem
Workload: 20% branches. Predictor accuracy: test 90%, 95%, 99%. Branch penalty on mispredict: 15 cycles. Without speculation stall per branch: 2 cycles. Processor can execute 4 instructions per cycle.

No-speculation branch penalty = branch_freq × stall = 0.20 × 2 = 0.40
Effective CPI without speculation = 0.25 + 0.40 = 0.65

With speculation:
Per-branch expected penalty = (1 - accuracy) × 15
Per-instruction penalty = branch_freq × per-branch penalty
Add to base CPI 0.25 to get effective CPI.

Compare effective CPIs to compute speedup = CPI_no_spec / CPI_with_spec

screens.title: Speculation Beyond Branches: Value and Cache-Line Prediction
screens.narratorSegment: Speculation extends past branch guessing. The chapter highlights three additional speculative areas: memory disambiguation (already covered), value prediction, and cache line prediction. Value prediction attempts to guess the result of an instruction before it executes. While promising in research, commercial processors rarely use aggressive value prediction because incorrect value guesses require re-execution and can be costly. Cache line prediction prefetches likely-needed cache lines based on access patterns; when accurate, it hides memory latency, but incorrect prefetches waste bandwidth and power. A concrete contrast: memory disambiguation speculation leverages address relationships and can forward data when correct. Value prediction guesses data values — if the guess is wrong, dependent instructions must be replayed. Cache-line prediction is cheaper to roll back because it is primarily a prefetch and only affects cache contents. A common misconception is that more speculation forms always stack to multiply performance; in reality, each adds cost and complexity, and interactions can reduce net benefit. The takeaway: architects evaluate each speculation form individually and in combination, focusing on workloads where the accuracy and recovery costs make them profitable. screens.title: Trade-offs: Accuracy, Recovery Cost, and Performance Gain
screens.narratorSegment: Designers must weigh three interdependent factors: accuracy, recovery cost, and performance gain. Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct; recovery cost is the cycles and resources lost when a speculation is wrong; performance gain is the time saved when a speculation is correct. Using the expected-gain inequality lets you combine these into a single decision metric. A concrete example repeated from the chapter: with 95% accuracy and a 15-cycle misprediction penalty, the expected cost per branch is 0.75 cycles — smaller than the expected 0.95-cycle gain from avoiding a one-cycle stall, so speculation is profitable. However, if recovery cost grows or accuracy drops, the same speculation becomes unprofitable. A common misconception is to optimize only for raw accuracy; sometimes reducing recovery cost (for example by faster pipeline refill or cheaper replay) is more effective than marginally improving accuracy. The takeaway is that architects tune predictors, ROB size, forwarding paths, and scheduling strategy together to maximize net benefit, and they may throttle speculation when security or power concerns dominate. screens.title: Limits of Speculation: Security, Power, and Diminishing Returns
screens.narratorSegment: Speculation improves performance but has practical limits. The chapter identifies three major boundaries. First, security vulnerabilities: speculative execution can leak information through microarchitectural state. The Spectre and Meltdown incidents showed that speculative side effects such as cache state can be probed to infer secrets, prompting a rethinking of speculation boundaries. Responses included hardware patches, software mitigations, and new hardware designs that isolate speculative state. Second, power consumption: speculative work consumes energy even when discarded, which is a significant concern for mobile and energy-constrained systems. Third, diminishing returns: as processors become more aggressive, prediction accuracy tends to fall and recovery costs often rise, limiting net gains. A common misconception is that more speculation is always better; in reality architects must trade some performance to improve security or reduce power. The takeaway is that speculation is not free — designers balance throughput against security risk and energy budget, sometimes deliberately reducing speculation in sensitive or low-power contexts. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we will explore why modern processors make educated guesses and how those guesses can both accelerate and complicate execution. Speculative execution lets a C P U execute instructions before dependencies or branch directions are certain. When predictions are correct, work is committed quickly and throughput rises. When predictions are wrong, the processor discards speculative results and pays a recovery cost. You will learn the role of the reorder buffer in delaying commits until program order is safe, how memory disambiguation allows loads to run early, and why techniques like store set prediction can improve or harm performance depending on accuracy. We will also quantify the trade-offs: accuracy versus recovery cost versus performance gain, using an expected-gain inequality to judge profitability. Finally, you will reflect on real limits — security issues such as Spectre and Meltdown, power consumption, and diminishing returns — and how architects balance speed and safety. By the end, you should be able to reason about when speculation is a net win and when designers must pull back.

By the end of this chapter you will confidently explain speculative execution and how it depends on branch prediction, describe the role and guarantees provided by the reorder buffer, and reason about memory disambiguation techniques used for speculative loads. You will also be able to analyze the trade-offs that make speculation profitable or not, using the expected-gain inequality to compare accuracy and recovery cost. Each objective pairs a precise skill with why it matters: being able to explain speculation helps you design or evaluate processor pipelines, understanding the ROB ensures you can reason about precise exceptions and correct commits, and mastering memory dependence techniques clarifies which workloads benefit most from aggressive speculation. Finally, you will reflect on practical limits — security vulnerabilities and power costs — and consider when designers must throttle speculation. These competencies prepare you to assess both performance gains and system risks in real hardware design or architecture evaluation.

This second objectives slide focuses on assessment and practical application. You will calculate expected performance using real numbers, make a judgment about whether memory-disambiguation speculation is profitable, and explain the implications of misprediction on CPI and pipeline refill cost. These skills are critical because the profitability of speculation is not binary — it depends on workload characteristics, predictor accuracy, and the cost to recover. For example, you will compute expected gain per speculation using the inequality Accuracy×Gain_when_correct > (1−Accuracy)×Cost_when_wrong, and then apply it to branch and load examples. You will also learn to spot common misconceptions: high raw accuracy alone is not enough if recovery cost is very large, and per-instruction gains may not translate to whole-program speedup if the instruction is off the critical path. These applied checks prepare you for architecture design trade-offs and evaluation tasks.

Speculative execution begins with branch prediction: the processor guesses which path a branch will take and continues fetching and executing instructions along that guessed path. Define speculative execution as executing instructions before their validity is confirmed, and branch prediction as the mechanism that makes the guesses. A concrete example: when a conditional jump depends on a register loaded from memory, early fetching of both the predicted path instructions and their operands keeps decode and execution units busy while the branch resolves. This produces performance when the predictor is correct because the pipeline avoids stalls and work is committed with little delay. A common misconception is to assume that speculative execution changes program semantics — it does not. Speculative results are kept separate from the architectural state until a commit, so incorrect speculations are discarded, and the program-level behavior remains the same. The key takeaway is that speculation increases throughput but requires mechanisms to track, validate, and discard work when predictions fail. Reflect: what kind of workload would gain most from accurate branch prediction? Branch Prediction & Speculative Execution — The Basics means speculative execution performs work based on predictions; correct predictions save cycles, incorrect ones require recovery but do not change program correctness.. In practical terms, how guessing branch outcomes keeps pipelines busy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The reorder buffer, or ROB, is the structure that lets processors execute out of order while still committing results in program order. Conceptually it is a circular buffer that holds each instruction from issue until commit. When an instruction completes out of order, its result is written into the ROB entry, not yet into the register file or memory. Only when the instruction reaches the head of the ROB and all prior instructions are committed does the processor write its result to the architectural state. This design guarantees precise exceptions: if an exception or misprediction occurs, the ROB can be flushed back to a known safe state because no speculative results have modified the visible state. A concrete example: a speculative instruction that computed a register value waits in the ROB; if the branch that enabled it mispredicts, that ROB entry is discarded and no architectural register is modified. A common misconception is that out-of-order execution commits results as they finish — it does not. The ROB is the gatekeeper. The main takeaway is that the ROB decouples execution completion from architectural commitment, enabling both performance and correctness.

Speculative state follows a lifecycle from fetch to commit. First, the branch predictor suggests a path and the fetch stage brings in instructions. Those instructions are allocated ROB entries and are allowed to execute out of order in reservation stations. When an instruction produces a result, it writes into its ROB slot marked speculative. The branch resolution event clears speculation bits if the path was correct; then entries become eligible to commit in program order. If the branch is wrong, all speculative ROB entries after the mispredicted branch are flushed and their work is discarded. Consider an example: a sequence of instructions after a predicted taken branch executes and populates ROB entries; branch resolves as not taken — the pipeline must discard those entries and fetch the right path, incurring refill latency. A common misconception is that flushing simply wastes a few cycles; in practice, the recovery cost includes pipeline refill, lost cache prefetch benefits, and wasted execution bandwidth. The takeaway: the lifecycle enforces correctness but determines recovery cost, so architects aim to reduce both misprediction rates and flush penalties.

Memory disambiguation addresses the question: can a load execute before earlier stores reveal their addresses? There are three primary strategies described in the chapter. First, address-based disambiguation compares computed store addresses against load addresses as soon as they become available. If they match, the load is re-executed or forwarded with correct data. This is precise but requires waiting for store addresses or checking them later. Second, store set prediction records which stores previously caused conflicts with a given load and predicts future conflicts, enabling the load to avoid executing early when likely to alias. This can increase performance if the predictor is accurate. Third, conservative scheduling simply delays loads until all prior store addresses are known; it is safe but limits parallelism. A concrete example: a load that frequently conflicts with a recent store benefits from store set prediction; a load that rarely aliases should be allowed early execution. A common misconception is thinking a single technique suits all workloads. In practice, architects combine mechanisms: fast predictions for common cases, precise checks to recover from mispredictions, and conservative fallbacks for uncertain situations. The takeaway is that memory-disambiguation design affects both performance and complexity.

Memory dependence speculation lets loads run before prior stores' addresses are known. This is powerful because many loads do not actually depend on earlier stores; running them early uncovers more instruction-level parallelism and often reduces critical-path latency. For a concrete example imagine a load whose address typically differs from recent stores; allowing it to run five cycles earlier can directly shorten execution time if the load lies on the critical path. The risk is that a misprediction requires the load and its dependent instructions to be replayed, which can be expensive. A common misconception is to assume all loads benefit equally; they do not. Only loads that are likely independent and on the critical path offer meaningful gains. The chapter emphasizes that accurate prediction and efficient forwarding or replay mechanisms are essential. The takeaway is simple: memory dependence speculation is one of the most performance-critical designs in aggressive out-of-order processors, and its profitability hinges on accurate conflict prediction and low replay cost. Here are three succinct concepts to anchor your memory. First, speculative execution: it executes instructions before their validity is confirmed, enabling higher throughput when predictions are right, but requiring rollback mechanisms when wrong. Second, the reorder buffer (ROB): it records speculative results and enforces in-order commits so architectural state remains correct and exceptions precise. Third, memory disambiguation: speculative loads depend on predicting whether earlier stores alias; techniques like address checks and store set prediction trade precision for performance. Keep these three concepts in mind when evaluating processor behavior: speculation gives performance, the ROB keeps correctness, and memory dependence prediction often yields the largest performance gains or losses.
